key: Hi, I’m Rosie. For nine years I’ve helped adults stop studying Chinese and start speaking it — professionals, expats, and heritage learners across 14 time zones. My whole method fits in one line: real conversation, from the very first 你好.

key: I grew up in Chengdu on teahouse gossip and spicy 串串 — switching between Sichuan dialect at the market and standard Mandarin at school. Language was never homework in our house. It was how you got the good stories.

key: Lessons are 80% you talking — even in week one, even when it comes out in fragments. I correct tones and grammar in the moment with a quick echo of the right version, so your flow never breaks, then send written notes afterwards so nothing is lost. Most students are holding a real, if wobbly, conversation by lesson three.

key: Before your first lesson I ask what you need Chinese for: the standup meeting, the in-laws in Hangzhou, the C-drama you watch without subtitles someday. Then we build from that material — your industry’s vocabulary, your neighbourhood, your group chat — because language you have a use for is language you keep.

key: Adults quit Chinese because being wrong out loud feels humiliating, not because tones are hard. So I never let a mistake become a moment. I mirror the correct form, we move on, and the same pattern quietly returns two lessons later until it sticks. You get precise feedback and keep your dignity.

key: I had tried three tutors and two apps before Rosie and always stalled at the same place — I could read and recognise plenty, but the second someone spoke to me my mind went blank and I reverted to English. What changed with Rosie is that she simply would not let the silence happen. She waits, she gives me the first two words, and somehow I finish the sentence myself. key: My daughter married into a Chinese family and I decided at 58 that I refused to be the silent grandmother at the table. Rosie built the whole first month around exactly that dinner table — the food words, the polite phrases, the questions relatives ask, even how to deflect the ones about my health. The first time I made my son-in-law’s mother laugh at something I said in Chinese, I cried in the car afterwards. That is not a language lesson, that is a family reunited.

key: I moved to Shenzhen for work with roughly forty words of Chinese and a lot of misplaced confidence. Rosie got me from surviving to actually enjoying the place — ordering properly, arguing with my landlord, making jokes badly. That is the part no app taught me.
